title: Exactors Who Glean the People
english: … gave.

Their aim, pursued with all their zeal, was to persuade people that the law had to be kept in these matters above all; of the other commandments they took little account. That is why the Savior himself said to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe dill and mint and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith” (Matthew 23:23).

So they were greedy for gain and lovers of money. At times they brought harsh penalties on those who slipped, so that by terrifying anyone accused of anything at all they might induce them to bring offerings, sometimes even beyond their means. That is why he says to those they wronged: “My people, your exactors glean you, and those who demand payment rule over you” (Isaiah 3:12).

By saying “people” he still gives Israel to understand that if they chose to turn to what pleases him, they would meet with his gentleness and love for humankind, and would not fall away altogether from their close bond with him.

By saying that the exactors glean, he shows how great their insatiable greed for gain was. In the cornfields some cut the ears with iron, while others gather the stalks that fall from the reaper’s hand and leave nothing in the fields. Those who harvest vines usually do the same. “So your exactors glean you,” he says. It is as if he said: They have harvested your wealth, and their greed does not stop there. They are already gleaning as well, that is, laying their hands even on what is still left.

Very well and fittingly he does not call them guides or teachers or anything of the kind; he names them exactors and collectors. He teaches that they lord it over the people, not dealing gently with them as teachers with disciples, but like harsh and savage masters, forcing them to think as they see fit and driving them to anything at all, at times even against their own judgment.

But the aim of those in Christ was not of this kind. The inspired Peter writes to those called to oversight, whose lot it is to lead the rational flocks: “not as lording it over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3).

The mystical sense also knows of other exactors, whom those who wish to live rightly must refuse. For the wicked and hostile powers all but demand of everyone on earth eagerness for what is base, and collect from us a kind of tribute: the mind’s leaning toward the passions. And indeed the holy … calls blessed …

title: Seven Women and One Man
english: … us in the spiritual strength of God who is over all, we keep safe in ourselves the bright beauty of our own nature. But when he withdraws his help, we shall be utterly stripped of every good; having lost the beauty of the glories that come from virtue, we shall be subject to dishonorable passions (Romans 1:26) and shall be slaves to enemies.
“And seven women will take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be called over us; take away our reproach” (Isaiah 4:1).

Having fully completed his account of the Jewish women who would go from luxury and wealth into captivity, he tries to show that the cities of Judea will be left empty of men, and will have a great scarcity of those who were once the finest fighters. For he had said, “All your strong men will fall by the sword” (Isaiah 3:25).

What, then, is the proof of what I have said? It is framed with great skill and elegance. The law given through Moses says to the sons of Israel, “There shall be no one childless or barren among you” (Deuteronomy 7:14). So among the Jews it was counted one of the worst reproaches for a woman not to bear children, or for any man to be childless; for at once the stigma of the childless and the barren was fastened on them.

The law was indeed spiritual (Romans 7:14). For the God of all was promising that the spiritual Israel, that is, the mind that sees God, would not be fruitless or made barren, but fruitful instead, like a good and choice land. But the Jews understood it in a fleshly way, for they were natural men, not having the Spirit (Jude 19).

So, he says, there will be such a scarcity of males in the land, once the war has consumed the race, that seven women, that is, many, will take hold of one man and say: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be called over us; take away our reproach.” Do you see how they dread the reproach of childlessness, and how strongly they refuse the name of childless and barren? For they come not seeking the usual things, what wives are accustomed to receive from their husbands; they say they will provide for themselves in this, and ask only, as I said, that their reproach be taken away.

Note the depth of the passage. If the man they appealed to had been rich, the women would not have said, “We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing.” But since they know that those who were saved from the war and barely escaped have fallen into utter poverty and great misery, they ask nothing at all of them, and seek only to become mothers of children.
That is the sense of the history. But they carry the passage before us over …

title: The Hedge Removed and the True Vine
english: … Israel has passed without holy prophets. At times they were taken captive and went off to the land of the Persians and Medes together with their wives and those dearest to them. Yet when the Babylonians had at one time taken the famous Jerusalem, they did not go down into Egypt without holy prophets: the prophet Jeremiah was with them, ministering the words that came from above and from God.

But since they raged against Christ, they have remained without a hedge, and all their security has fallen. This, I think, is what is meant by saying that its wall is pulled down (Isaiah 5:5). Every word of the holy prophets to them has ceased, held back in a way like rain (Isaiah 5:6), and the voices of the saints have failed.

And this, I think, is what God said to them through one of the prophets: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send a famine on the land, not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. And from the east to the west they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it” (Amos 8:11–12).

These things, as I said, have befallen those of Israel, and with good reason. For they thrust away the Lord of hosts, who waters souls and hearts in a spiritual way and enriches them with spiritual dews; blessed David also recalled these, saying, “Like the dew of Hermon that comes down on the mountains of Zion” (Psalm 133:3).

In its place a new vineyard has been raised up, made up of those called through faith to holiness. Of them the Bridegroom from heaven, that is, Christ, says: “The vines are in blossom; they have given their fragrance” (Song of Songs 2:13). He himself is the first, all-holy, and true vine, and we hang from him like branches, filled with the life-giving richness that comes from him.

Indeed, he said plainly: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that bears fruit he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–2).

Since we have grown onto him through kinship, clearly a spiritual kinship, we have been made fruitful. And he himself confirms us in this, saying: “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it abides in the vine, neither can you unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches. Whoever abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5).

So I say that we must hold fast, through faith and love and readiness to obey in everything, to the true vine, that is, Christ. For he will make us fruitful; he himself will set a hedge around us, raise up the wall, and drive …
